# Decisions

This project was built with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) in small steps. Each step was planned
together, then reviewed, tested and committed by me before the next one started.

---

## 1. What the AI generated vs. what I wrote

**The code was generated by the AI**: backend, frontend, migrations, seed data, tests and documentation.
My part was the direction: setting requirements, making the design decisions, reviewing each step, and
catching problems the AI did not raise.

| Area | My part | AI's part |
|---|---|---|
| **Duplicate distributions** | Decided that a track can be sent to each DSP only once | Unique index on (track, DSP), domain check with a clear message, tests |
| **Authentication** | Asked for a login endpoint that returns a JWT, a **Users table**, and a register/login popup shown when the site opens | Register/login API, JWT, password hashing, rate limiting, the popup |
| **`/api/auth/me`** | **Rejected it**: a returning user should simply sign in again | Had added it; removed it and kept the token in `sessionStorage` (cleared when the tab closes) |
| **Project structure** | Had the interfaces moved out of the service folders into their own folder | Clean Architecture layout; moved interfaces to `Application/Common/Interfaces` |
| **Audit trail** | Asked for a record of who created or changed what, and when | Audit columns, an `AuditLogs` table filled automatically on save, history endpoints, the History section in the UI |
| **Add and edit screens** | Noticed the UI was read-only and asked for add **and edit** on every screen | Edit endpoints, DSP list, artists page, add/edit popups, send-to-DSPs and status actions |
| **Genre** | Noticed genre was free text and chose a fixed list owned by the API | `GET /api/genres`, validation, dropdown |
| **Tools & scope** | Chose LocalDB (with SSMS instructions), the latest versions (.NET 10, Angular 21), a tight scope and simple tests | Setup, configuration, 57 unit tests |
| **Problems found while running it** | Reported Swagger not loading and the backend README missing | Found the causes and fixed them |

---

## 2. Security issues found or introduced, and how they were handled

**Found and fixed**

- **Vulnerable dependency.** SQL Server's client library pulled in `System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs` 9.0.11,
  which has known vulnerabilities (GHSA-846f-f764-76mx high, GHSA-2fmv-rv2c-59x7 moderate). The fixed version
  10.0.14 is pinned in `TrackManagement.Infrastructure.csproj`.
- **Brute-force login.** Register and login are limited to 10 requests per minute per IP. Further attempts get
  `429 Too many requests`.
- **User enumeration.** A wrong email and a wrong password return the same message. For an unknown email the
  API still runs a password-hash check, so the response time does not reveal whether the account exists.

**Prevented by design**

- **Secure by default.** Every endpoint requires a valid JWT unless it is explicitly marked anonymous. Only
  register and login are anonymous, plus Swagger in Development.
- **JWT validation.** Issuer, audience, lifetime (60 minutes) and signature are checked. Only HS256 is
  accepted, so a forged `alg: none` token is rejected; this was tested, along with a tampered token.
- **Signing key.** It is not in `appsettings.json`. The API refuses to start without a key of at least
  32 characters. Outside Development the key must come from an environment variable or a secret store.
- **Passwords.** Hashed with ASP.NET Core Identity's PBKDF2 hasher, never stored or logged in plain text.
  The audit trail skips the Users table and masks any password hash as `***`. This is covered by a test.
- **Input.** Every request body is validated and returns clear 400 errors. EF Core uses parameterised queries
  (no SQL injection), and unique indexes back up the duplicate checks.
- **Error details.** Unexpected errors return a generic 500 message. Stack traces only go to the server log.
- **CORS.** Only the Angular app (`http://localhost:4200`) may call the API from a browser.
- **Frontend.** The token is attached only to requests to our own API, never to other hosts. A `401` signs
  the user out.

**Accepted trade-offs (introduced knowingly)**

- **Token in `sessionStorage`.** A script injected into the page (XSS) could read it. This is limited by the
  60-minute expiry and Angular's automatic HTML escaping. An httpOnly cookie would be stronger but needs
  CSRF protection, which was out of scope.
- **Development secrets in the repository.** `appsettings.Development.json` holds a development signing key
  and the demo user's password, so a reviewer can run the app immediately. Both are used **only** in
  Development: the demo user is not created in any other environment.
- **In-memory rate limiting.** The counters reset when the API restarts and are not shared between
  servers. For production it would move to a shared store or the API gateway.

---

## 3. One thing the AI got wrong

**Every release date was shown one day early.**

On the track list, the AI formatted the release date with Angular's date pipe and added a `'UTC'` timezone
argument "so it never shifts a day". It did the opposite. Angular reads a plain date like `2025-08-30` as
*local* midnight. Converting that to UTC moved it back one day for anyone east of UTC, which includes Egypt
(UTC+2). So *Atlas*, released on 30 Aug 2025, was shown as **Aug 29, 2025**.

- **How it was caught:** by comparing the dates on the page with the database, not by trusting the code. The
  code looked correct and even had a comment explaining why it was "safe".
- **Fix:** the timezone argument was removed. All 10 tracks then matched the database exactly, and a comment
  in the template explains why there must be no timezone argument.
- **Lesson:** AI-written code can be confidently wrong in exactly the places it claims to be careful, and
  date/time handling is one of them. Checking real output against the source of truth is what caught it.

Other AI mistakes caught during the build: Swagger could not load because the HTTPS redirect ran in the
wrong order; the first audit migration would have stamped existing rows with the date `0001-01-01` and an
empty author; and an unneeded `/me` endpoint was added.

---

## Other key decisions

- **Status moves forward only, one step at a time:** Draft → Submitted → Distributed. Sending a track to DSPs
  moves a Draft to Submitted. Distributed requires the track to be Live on at least one DSP.
- **Live and Rejected are set by the DSPs**, so there is no endpoint or button to set them.
- **After Draft, a track's artist and ISRC are locked**, because the DSPs identify the recording by them.
  Title, genre and release date can still be edited.
- **Genres come from a fixed list owned by the API**, so near-duplicates ("Hip Hop" / "hip-hop") cannot
  break the genre filter.
- **The audit trail is written automatically on every save**, so no feature can forget to record a change.
  Seed data is inserted by a migration and therefore has no history.
- **ISRC** is accepted with or without dashes, stored as 12 upper-case characters, and unique.
- **Errors use ProblemDetails (RFC 7807)** with a status code per case: 400 invalid input, 401, 404, 409 for
  duplicates and business rules, and 429.
